claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection of macrophages reprograms cellular metabolism to promote lipid retention.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection of macrophages reprograms cellular metabolism to promote lipid retention.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Intracellular Mtb utilize host-derived lipids to maintain infection.
source: While it is clearly known that intracellular Mtb utilize host-derived lipids to maintain infection, the role of macrophage lipid processing on the bacteria's ability to access the intracellular lipid pool remains undefined.
evidence: This statement is described as 'clearly known' and is supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: Macrophages that cannot import, store, or catabolize fatty acids restrict Mtb growth by both common and divergent antimicrobial mechanisms.
source: Our analyses demonstrate that macrophages that cannot either import, store, or catabolize fatty acids restrict Mtb growth by both common and divergent antimicrobial mechanisms, including increased glycolysis, increased oxidative stress, production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, enhanced autophagy, and nutrient limitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including CFU counts, metabolic flux analyses, western blots, and RNA sequencing.

claim: Impaired macrophage lipid droplet biogenesis is restrictive to Mtb replication.
source: We also show that impaired macrophage lipid droplet biogenesis is restrictive to Mtb replication, but increased induction of the same fails to rescue Mtb growth.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data from Plin2-/- macrophages shown in Figure 1B and rescue experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Increased induction of lipid droplets fails to rescue Mtb growth.
source: We also show that impaired macrophage lipid droplet biogenesis is restrictive to Mtb replication, but increased induction of the same fails to rescue Mtb growth.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Cpt2-/- macrophages with increased lipid droplets still restrict Mtb growth (Figure 1B, Figure 4B).

claim: Mtb primarily infects macrophages in the lung.
source: Mtb primarily infects macrophages in the lung (Cohen et al., 2018; Wolf et al., 2007), wherein the bacterium relies on host-derived fatty acids and cholesterol for the synthesis of its lipid-rich cell wall and to produce energy and virulence factors (Peyron et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2012; Daniel et al., 2011; Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Brzostek et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2018 and Wolf et al., 2007.

claim: Mtb relies on host-derived fatty acids and cholesterol for the synthesis of its lipid-rich cell wall and to produce energy and virulence factors.
source: Mtb primarily infects macrophages in the lung (Cohen et al., 2018; Wolf et al., 2007), wherein the bacterium relies on host-derived fatty acids and cholesterol for the synthesis of its lipid-rich cell wall and to produce energy and virulence factors (Peyron et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2012; Daniel et al., 2011; Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Brzostek et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Peyron et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2012; Daniel et al., 2011; Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Brzostek et al., 2009.

claim: Resident alveolar macrophages preferentially oxidize fatty acids and are more permissive to Mtb growth.
source: Within the lung microenvironment, resident alveolar macrophages preferentially oxidize fatty acids and are more permissive to Mtb growth while recruited interstitial macrophages are more glycolytic and restrictive of Mtb replication (Huang et al., 2018; Pisu et al., 2020; Pisu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2018; Pisu et al., 2020; Pisu et al., 2021.

claim: Recruited interstitial macrophages are more glycolytic and restrictive of Mtb replication.
source: Within the lung microenvironment, resident alveolar macrophages preferentially oxidize fatty acids and are more permissive to Mtb growth while recruited interstitial macrophages are more glycolytic and restrictive of Mtb replication (Huang et al., 2018; Pisu et al., 2020; Pisu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2018; Pisu et al., 2020; Pisu et al., 2021.

claim: Mtb-infected macrophages shift their mitochondrial substrate preference to exogenous fatty acids.
source: Mtb-infected macrophages shift their mitochondrial substrate preference to exogenous fatty acids, which drives the formation of foamy macrophages that are laden with cytosolic lipid droplets (Peyron et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2009; Cumming et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2012; Podinovskaia et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peyron et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2009; Cumming et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2012; Podinovskaia et al., 2013.

claim: The shift in mitochondrial substrate preference to exogenous fatty acids drives the formation of foamy macrophages that are laden with cytosolic lipid droplets.
source: Mtb-infected macrophages shift their mitochondrial substrate preference to exogenous fatty acids, which drives the formation of foamy macrophages that are laden with cytosolic lipid droplets (Peyron et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2009; Cumming et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2012; Podinovskaia et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peyron et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2009; Cumming et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2012; Podinovskaia et al., 2013.

claim: Foamy macrophages are found in abundance in the central and inner layers of granulomas.
source: Foamy macrophages are found in abundance in the central and inner layers of granulomas, a common histopathological feature of human TB (Russell et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Russell et al., 2009 and Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Interference with key regulators of lipid homeostasis enhances macrophage control of Mtb.
source: Interference with key regulators of lipid homeostasis, such as the miR-33 and the transcription factors peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα) and PPAR-γ, enhances macrophage control of Mtb (Kim et al., 2017; Almeida et al., 2009; Ouimet et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2017; Almeida et al., 2009; Ouimet et al., 2016.

claim: Metformin and some cholesterol-lowering drugs are under investigation for host-directed therapeutics against Mtb.
source: Moreover, compounds that modulate lipid metabolism such as the antidiabetic drug metformin and some cholesterol-lowering drugs are under investigation for host-directed therapeutics (HDTs) against Mtb (Parihar et al., 2014; Singhal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parihar et al., 2014 and Singhal et al., 2014.

claim: In Mtb-infected foamy macrophages, bacteria containing phagosomes are found in close apposition to intracellular lipid droplets.
source: In Mtb-infected foamy macrophages, bacteria containing phagosomes are found in close apposition to intracellular lipid droplets (Peyron et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peyron et al., 2008.

claim: Intracellular Mtb has been shown to import fatty acids from host lipid droplet-derived triacylglycerols.
source: In fact, intracellular Mtb has been shown to import fatty acids from host lipid droplet- derived triacylglycerols (Daniel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Daniel et al., 2011.

claim: Macrophage lipid droplet formation in response to Mtb infection can lead to the induction of a protective, antimicrobial response.
source: However, other studies indicate that macrophage lipid droplet formation in response to Mtb infection can lead to the induction of a protective, antimicrobial response (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knight et al., 2018.

claim: Mtb appears unable to acquire host lipids when lipid droplets are induced by stimulation with interferon gamma (IFN-γ).
source: Mtb appears unable to acquire host lipids when lipid droplets are induced by stimulation with interferon gamma (IFN-γ) (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knight et al., 2018.

claim: Lipid droplets can be sites for the production of host-protective pro-inflammatory eicosanoids.
source: Moreover, there is some evidence that lipid droplets can be sites for the production of host-protective pro-inflammatory eicosanoids (Knight et al., 2018; Daniel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knight et al., 2018 and Daniel et al., 2011.

claim: Lipid droplets can act as innate immune hubs against intracellular bacterial pathogens by clustering antibacterial proteins.
source: Lipid droplets can also act as innate immune hubs against intracellular bacterial pathogens by clustering antibacterial proteins (Bosch et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bosch et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibition of macrophage fatty acid oxidation by knocking out mitochondrial carnitine palmitoyl transferase 2 (CPT2) restricts intracellular growth of Mtb.
source: Inhibition of macrophage fatty acid oxidation by knocking out mitochondrial carnitine palmitoyl transferase 2 (CPT2) or using chemical inhibitors of CPT2 also restrict intracellular growth of Mtb (Chandra et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chandra et al., 2020 and Huang et al., 2018.

claim: Using chemical inhibitors of CPT2 restricts intracellular growth of Mtb.
source: Inhibition of macrophage fatty acid oxidation by knocking out mitochondrial carnitine palmitoyl transferase 2 (CPT2) or using chemical inhibitors of CPT2 also restrict intracellular growth of Mtb (Chandra et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chandra et al., 2020 and Huang et al., 2018.

claim: Deletion of CD36 or CPT2 in mouse macrophages has been shown to impair intracellular growth of Mtb.
source: Deletion of CD36 or CPT2 in mouse macrophages has been shown to impair intracellular growth of Mtb (Hawkes et al., 2010; Chandra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hawkes et al., 2010 and Chandra et al., 2020.

claim: SLC27A1 and SLC27A4 are the most abundant fatty acid transporter isoforms in macrophages.
source: SLC27A1 and SLC27A4 are the most abundant fatty acid transporter isoforms in macrophages (Nishiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nishiyama et al., 2018.

claim: PLIN2 is known to be required for lipid droplet formation.
source: PLIN2, or adipophilin, is known to be required for lipid droplet formation (Paul et al., 2008; Larigauderie et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Paul et al., 2008 and Larigauderie et al., 2004.

claim: PLIN2 is the dominant isoform expressed in macrophages among five isoforms of mammalian perilipins involved in lipid droplet biogenesis.
source: Five isoforms of mammalian perilipins (PLIN) are involved in lipid droplet biogenesis among which PLIN2 is the dominant isoform expressed in macrophages (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knight et al., 2018.

claim: Macrophages derived from Plin2-/- mice show no defects in the production of lipid droplets.
source: However, macrophages derived from Plin2-/- mice show no defects in the production of lipid droplets nor do they impair intracellular growth of Mtb (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knight et al., 2018.

claim: Macrophages derived from Plin2-/- mice do not impair intracellular growth of Mtb.
source: However, macrophages derived from Plin2-/- mice show no defects in the production of lipid droplets nor do they impair intracellular growth of Mtb (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knight et al., 2018.

claim: Each individual sgRNA achieved >85% CRISPR-mediated deletion efficiency for all five genes.
source: Each individual sgRNA achieved >85% CRISPR-mediated deletion efficiency for all the five genes as analyzed by the Inference for CRISPR Edits (ICE) tool (Conant et al., 2022; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analyzed using the ICE tool and presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: All five mutant macrophages significantly impaired Mtb growth rates compared to scrambled sgRNA as assessed by CFU counts on day 5.
source: All the five mutant macrophages significantly impaired Mtb growth rates compared to scrambled sgRNA as assessed by CFUs counts on day 5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Plin2-/-, Slc27a1-/-, and Cpt2-/- macrophages displayed the strongest growth restriction phenotypes.
source: Plin2-/-, Slc27a1-/-, and Cpt2-/- macrophages displayed the strongest growth restriction phenotypes while Cd36-/-macrophages had a moderate, but significant, impact on Mtb growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cd36-/- macrophages had a moderate, but significant, impact on Mtb growth.
source: Plin2-/-, Slc27a1-/-, and Cpt2-/- macrophages displayed the strongest growth restriction phenotypes while Cd36-/-macrophages had a moderate, but significant, impact on Mtb growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The moderate growth restriction phenotypes of Cd36-/- macrophages were consistent with previous findings.
source: The moderate growth restriction phenotypes of Cd36-/- macrophages were consistent with previous findings, which reported a similar impact on Mtb and M. marinum growth in macrophages derived from Cd36-/- mice (Hawkes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim compares current experimental results with previous findings cited from Hawkes et al., 2010.

claim: Impaired growth of Mtb in Cpt1a-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages is consistent with previous reports that genetic and chemical inhibition of fatty acid oxidation is detrimental to the growth of Mtb within macrophages.
source: Impaired growth of Mtb in Cpt1a-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages is also consistent with previous reports that genetic and chemical inhibition of fatty acid oxidation is detrimental to the growth of Mtb within macrophages (Huang et al., 2018; Chandra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim compares current experimental results with previous findings cited from Huang et al., 2018 and Chandra et al., 2020.

claim: Plin2-/- macrophages displayed a complete absence of lipid droplet formation compared to controls.
source: We observed a complete absence of lipid droplet formation in Plin2-/- macrophages compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: This is contrary to previous observations in macrophages derived from PLIN2 knockout mice, which were reported to have no defect in lipid droplet formation.
source: This is contrary to previous observations in macrophages derived from PLIN2 knockout mice, which were reported to have no defect in lipid droplet formation (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim contrasts current findings with previous observations cited from Knight et al., 2018.

claim: CPT2 knockout in Cpt2-/- macrophages impaired the cell's ability to oxidize palmitate to a degree comparable to etomoxir treatment.
source: CPT2 knockout in Cpt2-/- macrophages impaired the cell's ability to oxidize palmitate to a degree comparable to etomoxir treatment as evidenced by baseline OCRs compared to scrambled sgRNA control (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse fatty acid oxidation analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Deletion of SLC27A1 knockout in macrophages rewires their substrate bias from fatty acids to glucose.
source: Impairment of fatty acids metabolism by SLC27A1 knockout in macrophages rewires their substrate bias from fatty acids to glucose (Johnson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2016.

claim: All three mutant uninfected macrophages displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration as evidenced by lower basal and spare respiratory capacity compared to scrambled sgRNA controls.
source: All three mutant uninfected macrophages displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration as evidenced by lower basal and spare respiratory capacity (SRC) compared to scrambled sgRNA controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mtb infection proportionally reduced basal and SRC rates across all the mutant macrophages and scrambled controls compared to uninfected macrophages.
source: Mtb infection proportionally reduced basal and SRC rates across all the mutant macrophages and scrambled controls (Figure 2A and B) compared to uninfected macrophages, which is consistent with previous findings (Cumming et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2A and B and is consistent with previous findings cited from Cumming et al., 2018.

claim: Plin2-/- macrophages displayed the most marked reduction in mitochondrial activity in both uninfected and infected conditions.
source: Plin2-/- macrophages displayed the most marked reduction in mitochondrial activity in both uninfected and infected conditions, while Slc27a1-/- macrophages were the least affected (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Uninfected Slc27a1-/- macrophages were more glycolytically active with higher basal and spare glycolytic capacity compared to scrambled controls.
source: As reported previously (Johnson et al., 2016), uninfected Slc27a1-/- macrophages were more glycolytically active with higher basal and spare glycolytic capacity (SGC) compared to scrambled controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D and is consistent with previous findings cited from Johnson et al., 2016.

claim: Uninfected Plin2-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages were more glycolytically active, but to a greater degree than Slc27a1-/-.
source: Uninfected Plin2-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages were also more glycolytically active, but to a greater degree than Slc27a1-/- (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Mtb infection increased the glycolytic capacity of all three mutant macrophages.
source: Mtb infection increased the glycolytic capacity of all the three mutant macrophages (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Plin2-/- macrophages exhibited the highest glycolytic capacity.
source: Overall, Plin2-/- macrophages exhibited the highest glycolytic capacity (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Increased glycolytic flux in macrophages has been linked to the control of intracellular Mtb growth.
source: Increased glycolytic flux in macrophages has been linked to the control of intracellular Mtb growth (Gleeson et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gleeson et al., 2016 and Shi et al., 2015.

claim: Mtb infection is known to induce increased glycolysis or the 'Warburg effect' in macrophages, mouse lungs, and human TB granulomas.
source: Mtb infection is known to induce increased glycolysis or the 'Warburg effect' in macrophages, mouse lungs, and human TB granulomas (Shi et al., 2015; Gleeson et al., 2016; Belton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2015; Gleeson et al., 2016; Belton et al., 2016.

claim: The Warburg effect is mediated by the master transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF1).
source: Several studies have demonstrated that the Warburg effect is mediated by the master transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF1) (Courtnay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Courtnay et al., 2015.

claim: During Mtb infection, HIF1 is activated by the production of ROS, tricarboxylic cycle (TCA) intermediates and hypoxia in the cellular microenvironments.
source: During Mtb infection, HIF1 is activated by the production of ROS, tricarboxylic cycle (TCA) intermediates and hypoxia in the cellular microenvironments as a consequence of altered metabolic activities and increased immune cell functions (Li et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2015; Gleeson et al., 2016; Belton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2015; Gleeson et al., 2016; Belton et al., 2016.

claim: All three mutant macrophages displayed significantly higher amounts of total HIF1α compared to scrambled controls after Mtb infection for 48 hours.
source: Indeed, all the three mutant macrophages displayed significantly higher amounts of total HIF1α compared to scrambled controls after Mtb infection for 48 hours (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Slc27a1-/- and Plin2-/- macrophages had increased levels of total HIF1α even in uninfected states.
source: Slc27a1-/-, Plin2-/- macrophages had increased levels of total HIF1α even in uninfected states (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 3A and B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: AMPK is a master regulator of cell energy homeostasis.
source: We also checked the phosphorylation status of the adenosine monophosphate kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cell energy homeostasis (Garcia and Shaw, 2017), in the mutant macrophages since Seahorse flux analyses indicated that they had impaired mitochondrial activities (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garcia and Shaw, 2017.

claim: In both Mtb-infected and uninfected conditions, impaired fatty acid metabolism in the mutant macrophages correlated with increased activation of AMPK as indicated by higher levels of phosphorylated AMPK compared to scramble.
source: Western blot analysis revealed that in both Mtb-infected and uninfected conditions, impaired fatty acid metabolism in the mutant macrophages correlated with increased activation of AMPK as indicated by higher levels of phosphorylated AMPK compared to scramble (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 3C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Total AMPK was increased in Slc27a1-/- and Plin2-/- macrophages in both uninfected and Mtb-infected conditions.
source: Interestingly, total AMPK was also increased, at least in Slc27a1-/-and Plin2-/- macrophages, in both uninfected and Mtb-infected conditions (Figure 3C and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 3C and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Activated AMPK promotes catabolic processes such as autophagy to maintain nutrient supply and energy homeostasis in energetically stressed cellular environments.
source: In energetically stressed cellular environments, activated AMPK promotes catabolic processes such as autophagy to maintain nutrient supply and energy homeostasis (Garcia and Shaw, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garcia and Shaw, 2017.

claim: Autophagy is an innate immune defense mechanism against intracellular Mtb in macrophages.
source: Autophagy is also an innate immune defense mechanism against intracellular Mtb in macrophages (Gutierrez et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gutierrez et al., 2004.

claim: There was an increase in autophagic flux by western blot analysis of LC3II/LC3I ratios in Mtb-infected Slc27a1-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages.
source: We observed an increase in autophagic flux by western blot analysis of LC3II/LC3I ratios in Mtb-infected Slc27a1-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Cpt2-/- macrophages were more autophagic even in uninfected conditions.
source: Cpt2-/- macrophages were more autophagic even in uninfected conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Four autophagy genes (AMBRA1, ATG7, MAP1LC3B and ULK1) were upregulated in both Mtb-infected and uninfected conditions in all three mutants.
source: Meanwhile, our qPCR analysis also revealed that the four autophagy genes were upregulated in both Mtb-infected and uninfected conditions in all the three mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Inhibition of fatty acid oxidation enhances macrophage xenophagic activity, which leads to improved control of Mtb.
source: These data agree with previous observations that inhibition of fatty acid oxidation enhances macrophage xenophagic activity, which leads to improved control of Mtb (Chandra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chandra et al., 2020.

claim: The mycobacterial isocitrate lyase (icl1) acts as an isocitrate lyase in the glyoxylate shunt and as a methyl-isocitrate lyase in the methyl-citrate cycle (MCC).
source: The mycobacterial isocitrate lyase (icl1) acts as an isocitrate lyase in the glyoxylate shunt and as a methyl-isocitrate lyase in the methyl-citrate cycle (MCC) (Gould et al., 2006; McKinney et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gould et al., 2006 and McKinney et al., 2000.

claim: Mtb uses the MCC to convert propionyl CoA originating from the breakdown of cholesterol rings and β-oxidation of odd chain fatty acids into succinate and pyruvate, which are eventually assimilated into the tricarboxylic cycle (TCA).
source: Mtb uses the MCC to convert propionyl CoA originating from the breakdown of cholesterol rings and β-oxidation of odd chain fatty acids into succinate and pyruvate, which are eventually assimilated into the tricarboxylic cycle (TCA) (Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006; Griffin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006 and Griffin et al., 2012.

claim: The buildup of propionyl CoA is toxic to Mtb.
source: The buildup of propionyl CoA is toxic to Mtb and the bacteria relies on the MCC together with the incorporation of propionyl CoA to methyl-branched lipids in the cell wall as an internal detoxification system (Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006; Savvi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006 and Savvi et al., 2008.

claim: Mtb relies on the MCC together with the incorporation of propionyl CoA to methyl-branched lipids in the cell wall as an internal detoxification system.
source: The buildup of propionyl CoA is toxic to Mtb and the bacteria relies on the MCC together with the incorporation of propionyl CoA to methyl-branched lipids in the cell wall as an internal detoxification system (Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006; Savvi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006 and Savvi et al., 2008.

claim: Mtb propionyl CoA toxicity is, in part, due to a cellular imbalance between propionyl CoA and acetyl CoA as an accumulation of the former or paucity of the latter results in the propionyl CoA-mediated inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase.
source: Mtb propionyl CoA toxicity is, in part, due to a cellular imbalance between propionyl CoA and acetyl CoA as an accumulation of the former or paucity of the latter results in the propionyl CoA-mediated inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Mtb icl1-deficient mutants (Mtb Δicl1) are unable to grow in media supplemented with cholesterol or propionate, or intracellularly in macrophages.
source: Consequently, Mtb icl1-deficient mutants (Mtb Δicl1) are unable to grow in media supplemented with cholesterol or propionate, or intracellularly in macrophages (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: The growth inhibition of Mtb Δicl1 could be rescued both in culture and in macrophages by exogenous supply of acetate or even chain fatty acids, which can be oxidized to acetyl-CoA.
source: However, this growth inhibition could be rescued both in culture and in macrophages by exogenous supply of acetate or even chain fatty acids, which can be oxidized to acetyl-CoA (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: The Mtb Δicl1 mutant failed to replicate in both mutant and scramble macrophages that were grown in normal macrophage media.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Lee et al., 2013), the Mtb Δicl1 mutant failed to replicate in both mutant and scramble macrophages that were grown in normal macrophage media as evidenced by baseline mCherry fluorescence (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with previous observations cited from Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Oleate supplementation successfully rescued the Mtb Δicl1 mutant in scrambled control macrophages.
source: Oleate supplementation successfully rescued the Mtb Δicl1 mutant in scrambled control macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The growth restriction of the Mtb Δicl1 strain could not be alleviated by exogenous addition of oleate to the mutant macrophages (Slc27a1-/-, Plin2-/-, and Cpt2-/-).
source: However, the growth restriction of the Mtb Δicl1 strain could not be alleviated by exogenous addition of oleate to the mutant macrophages (Slc27a1-/-, Plin2-/-, and Cpt2-/-) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Oleate supplementation in macrophages induces the formation of lipid droplets.
source: Oleate supplementation in macrophages induces the formation of lipid droplets, and we were able to confirm the inability to produce lipid droplets in Plin2-/- macrophages using this approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Slc27a1-/- macrophages fail to generate lipid droplets upon oleate supplementation.
source: Confocal analysis of BODIPY-stained cells upon oleate supplementation revealed that Slc27a1-/- macrophages also fail to generate lipid droplets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cpt2-/- macrophages produced more and larger lipid droplets in comparison to scrambled controls upon oleate supplementation.
source: In contrast, Cpt2-/- macrophages produced more and larger lipid droplets in comparison to scrambled controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a clustering of all three mutant macrophages away from scrambled controls in principal component analysis of host transcriptomes.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of host transcriptomes revealed a clustering of all the three mutant macrophages away from scrambled controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a separation in transcriptional responses between the three mutant macrophages as Cpt2-/- and Plin2-/- macrophages clustered closer together and more distant from Slc27a1-/-.
source: Interestingly, there was a separation in transcriptional responses between the three mutant macrophages as Cpt2-/- and Plin2-/- macrophages clustered closer together and more distant from Slc27a1-/- (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 900 genes were differentially expressed in Plin2-/- macrophages (589 up, 311 down).
source: Overall, using an adjusted p-value<0.05 and absolute log2 fold change >1.2, we identified 900 genes that were differentially expressed (DE) in Plin2-/- macrophages (589 up, 311 down), 817 genes that were DE in Slc27a1-/- macrophages (501 up, 315 down), and 189 genes that were DE in Cpt2-/- (124 up, 65 down) (Supplementary file 2, Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5B.

claim: 817 genes were differentially expressed in Slc27a1-/- macrophages (501 up, 315 down).
source: Overall, using an adjusted p-value<0.05 and absolute log2 fold change >1.2, we identified 900 genes that were differentially expressed (DE) in Plin2-/- macrophages (589 up, 311 down), 817 genes that were DE in Slc27a1-/- macrophages (501 up, 315 down), and 189 genes that were DE in Cpt2-/- (124 up, 65 down) (Supplementary file 2, Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5B.

claim: 189 genes were differentially expressed in Cpt2-/- macrophages (124 up, 65 down).
source: Overall, using an adjusted p-value<0.05 and absolute log2 fold change >1.2, we identified 900 genes that were differentially expressed (DE) in Plin2-/- macrophages (589 up, 311 down), 817 genes that were DE in Slc27a1-/- macrophages (501 up, 315 down), and 189 genes that were DE in Cpt2-/- (124 up, 65 down) (Supplementary file 2, Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5B.

claim: Defects in fatty acid uptake in Slc27a1-/--infected macrophages upregulated pro-inflammatory pathways involved in MAPK and ERK signaling and production of inflammatory cytokines (IFN‐γ, IL-6, IL-1α, β).
source: We found that defects in fatty acid uptake in Slc27a1-/--infected macrophages upregulated pro-inflammatory pathways involved in MAPK and ERK signaling and production of inflammatory cytokines (IFN‐γ, IL-6, IL-1α, β) (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The pro-inflammatory signatures of the Slc27a1-/- macrophages are consistent with previous observations that demonstrated that a deficiency in Slc27a1-/- exacerbated macrophage activation in vitro and in vivo.
source: The pro-inflammatory signatures of the Slc27a1-/- macrophages are consistent with previous observations that demonstrated that a deficiency in Slc27a1-/- exacerbated macrophage activation in vitro and in vivo (Johnson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim compares current findings with previous observations cited from Johnson et al., 2016.

claim: Mtb-infected Slc27a1-/- macrophages showed reduced expression of other solute carrier transporters (SLC) such as SLC27A4, GLUT1 (SLC2A1), and eight SLC amino acid transporters.
source: SLC27A1 is a solute carrier family member transporter and Mtb-infected Slc27a1-/- macrophages showed reduced expression of other solute carrier transporters (SLC) such as SLC27A4, GLUT1 (SLC2A1), and eight SLC amino acid transporters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B and 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B and 2A, and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Mtb-infected Slc27a1-/- macrophage transcriptomes exhibited upregulation of macrophage scavenger receptors (MSR1) and the ATP binding cassette transporter ABCC1.
source: Interestingly, Mtb-infected Slc27a1-/- macrophage transcriptomes exhibited upregulation of macrophage scavenger receptors (MSR1) and the ATP binding cassette transporter ABCC1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), both of which can independently transport fatty acids into cells (Vogel et al., 2022; Raggers et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citations to Vogel et al., 2022 and Raggers et al., 1999.

claim: MSR1 and ABCC1 can independently transport fatty acids into cells.
source: Interestingly, Mtb-infected Slc27a1-/- macrophage transcriptomes exhibited upregulation of macrophage scavenger receptors (MSR1) and the ATP binding cassette transporter ABCC1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), both of which can independently transport fatty acids into cells (Vogel et al., 2022; Raggers et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vogel et al., 2022 and Raggers et al., 1999.

claim: Mtb infection of Plin2-/- macrophages led to upregulation in pathways involved in ribosomal biology, MHC class 1 antigen presentation, canonical glycolysis, ATP metabolic processes, and type 1 interferon responses.
source: Meanwhile, Mtb infection of Plin2-/- macrophages led to upregulation in pathways involved in ribosomal biology, MHC class 1 antigen presentation, canonical glycolysis, ATP metabolic processes, and type 1 interferon responses (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: In the downregulated Plin2-/- DE gene set, enriched pathways included those involved in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines; IL-6 and 8, IFN‐γ and IL-1.
source: In the downregulated Plin2-/- DE gene set, enriched pathways included those involved in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines; IL-6 and 8, IFN‐γ and IL-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation and processes involved in the respiratory chain electron transport were significantly enriched in Plin2-/- downregulated genes.
source: Oxidative phosphorylation and processes involved in the respiratory chain electron transport were also significantly enriched in Plin2-/- downregulated genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Mtb-infected Plin2-/- macrophages increase glycolytic flux and decrease mitochondrial activities.
source: This suggests that Mtb-infected Plin2-/- macrophages increase glycolytic flux and decrease mitochondrial activities, which is consistent with our metabolic flux analysis data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is an inference from RNA sequencing data that is consistent with Seahorse flux analysis data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plin2-/- macrophages are broadly anti-inflammatory as most pro-inflammatory genes were downregulated upon Mtb infection.
source: Unlike Slc27a1-/- macrophages, Plin2-/- macrophages are, however, broadly anti-inflammatory as most pro-inflammatory genes were downregulated upon Mtb infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data showing downregulation of pro-inflammatory pathways.

claim: Inhibition of fatty acid oxidation in Cpt2-/- macrophages upregulated pathways involved in MHC class 1 antigen presentation, response to IFN‐γ and IL-1 and T-cell-mediated immunity.
source: Further downstream in the lipid processing steps, inhibition of fatty acid oxidation in Cpt2-/- macrophages upregulated pathways involved in MHC class 1 antigen presentation, response to IFN‐γ and IL-1 and T-cell-mediated immunity (Figure 6—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Both Mtb-infected Plin2-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages were downregulated in the expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Similarly, both Mtb-infected Plin2-/- and Cpt2-/- macrophages were downregulated in the expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: 4 hours post infection, IL-1β and IFN-β were both upregulated in Slc27a1-/- macrophages compared to scrambled controls.
source: Indeed, 4 hours post infection, IL-1β and IFN-β were both upregulated in Slc27a1-/- macrophages compared to scrambled controls consistent with their pro-inflammatory phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: Plin2-/- macrophages downregulated IL-1β.
source: On the contrary, Plin2-/- macrophages downregulated IL-1β (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: 0 genes were differentially expressed in Mtb from Slc27a1-/- macrophages.
source: Using an adjusted p-value of <0.1 and an absolute log2 fold change >1.4, 0 genes were DE in Slc27a1-/- macrophages, 105 Mtb genes were DE in Plin2-/- macrophages (69 up, 36 down), and 10 genes were DE in Cpt2-/- macrophages (3 up, 7 down) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing analysis of bacterial transcriptomes presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: 105 Mtb genes were differentially expressed in Plin2-/- macrophages (69 up, 36 down).
source: Using an adjusted p-value of <0.1 and an absolute log2 fold change >1.4, 0 genes were DE in Slc27a1-/- macrophages, 105 Mtb genes were DE in Plin2-/- macrophages (69 up, 36 down), and 10 genes were DE in Cpt2-/- macrophages (3 up, 7 down) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing analysis of bacterial transcriptomes presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: 10 genes were differentially expressed in Mtb from Cpt2-/- macrophages (3 up, 7 down).
source: Using an adjusted p-value of <0.1 and an absolute log2 fold change >1.4, 0 genes were DE in Slc27a1-/- macrophages, 105 Mtb genes were DE in Plin2-/- macrophages (69 up, 36 down), and 10 genes were DE in Cpt2-/- macrophages (3 up, 7 down) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing analysis of bacterial transcriptomes presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Plin2-/- macrophages appeared to elicit the strongest transcriptional response from Mtb.
source: Plin2-/- macrophages appeared to elicit the strongest transcriptional response from Mtb, which is consistent with our CFU data (Figure 1B) as Plin2-/- macrophages exhibited the strongest growth restriction.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data showing the highest number of differentially expressed genes in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages and is consistent with CFU data in Figure 1B.

claim: Among the DE genes in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages, a significant number of upregulated genes are involved in nutrient assimilation.
source: Among the DE genes in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages (Supplementary file 4), a significant number of upregulated genes are involved in nutrient assimilation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Mtb in Plin2-/- macrophages upregulated CobU (Rv0254c), which is predicted to be involved in the bacteria's cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis.
source: Mtb in Plin2-/- macrophages upregulated CobU (Rv0254c), which is predicted to be involved in the bacteria's cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Vitamin B12 is an important cofactor for the activity of Mtb genes required for cholesterol and fatty acid utilization.
source: Vitamin B12 is an important cofactor for the activity of Mtb genes required for cholesterol and fatty acid utilization (Campos-Pardos et al., 2024; Savvi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Campos-Pardos et al., 2024 and Savvi et al., 2008.

claim: Genes involved in de novo long-chain fatty acid synthesis (AccE5, Rv281) were upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages.
source: Genes involved in de novo long-chain fatty acid synthesis (AccE5, Rv281) (Bazet Lyonnet et al., 2014), cholesterol breakdown (HsaD, Rv3569c) (Lack et al., 2010), β-oxidation of fatty acids (EchA18, Rv3373; FadE22, Rv3061c) (Schnappinger et al., 2003), purine salvage (Apt, Rv2584c) (Warner et al., 2014), and tryptophan metabolism (Lott, 2020) were also upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Bazet Lyonnet et al., 2014.

claim: Genes involved in cholesterol breakdown (HsaD, Rv3569c) were upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages.
source: Genes involved in de novo long-chain fatty acid synthesis (AccE5, Rv281) (Bazet Lyonnet et al., 2014), cholesterol breakdown (HsaD, Rv3569c) (Lack et al., 2010), β-oxidation of fatty acids (EchA18, Rv3373; FadE22, Rv3061c) (Schnappinger et al., 2003), purine salvage (Apt, Rv2584c) (Warner et al., 2014), and tryptophan metabolism (Lott, 2020) were also upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Lack et al., 2010.

claim: Genes involved in β-oxidation of fatty acids (EchA18, Rv3373; FadE22, Rv3061c) were upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages.
source: Genes involved in de novo long-chain fatty acid synthesis (AccE5, Rv281) (Bazet Lyonnet et al., 2014), cholesterol breakdown (HsaD, Rv3569c) (Lack et al., 2010), β-oxidation of fatty acids (EchA18, Rv3373; FadE22, Rv3061c) (Schnappinger et al., 2003), purine salvage (Apt, Rv2584c) (Warner et al., 2014), and tryptophan metabolism (Lott, 2020) were also upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Schnappinger et al., 2003.

claim: Genes involved in purine salvage (Apt, Rv2584c) were upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages.
source: Genes involved in de novo long-chain fatty acid synthesis (AccE5, Rv281) (Bazet Lyonnet et al., 2014), cholesterol breakdown (HsaD, Rv3569c) (Lack et al., 2010), β-oxidation of fatty acids (EchA18, Rv3373; FadE22, Rv3061c) (Schnappinger et al., 2003), purine salvage (Apt, Rv2584c) (Warner et al., 2014), and tryptophan metabolism (Lott, 2020) were also upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Warner et al., 2014.

claim: Genes involved in tryptophan metabolism were upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages.
source: Genes involved in de novo long-chain fatty acid synthesis (AccE5, Rv281) (Bazet Lyonnet et al., 2014), cholesterol breakdown (HsaD, Rv3569c) (Lack et al., 2010), β-oxidation of fatty acids (EchA18, Rv3373; FadE22, Rv3061c) (Schnappinger et al., 2003), purine salvage (Apt, Rv2584c) (Warner et al., 2014), and tryptophan metabolism (Lott, 2020) were also upregulated in Mtb from Plin2-/- macrophages (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Lott, 2020.

claim: This metabolic realignment response is seen most frequently under nutrient-limiting conditions.
source: This metabolic realignment response is seen most frequently under nutrient-limiting conditions (Huang et al., 2018; Pisu et al., 2020; Theriault et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2018; Pisu et al., 2020; Theriault et al., 2022.

claim: Mtb in Plin2-/- macrophages appears to experience a significant level of cellular stresses as genes involved in DNA synthesis and repair, general response to oxidative stress and pH survival in the phagosome were upregulated.
source: Mtb in Plin2-/- macrophages also appears to experience a significant level of other cellular stresses as genes involved in DNA synthesis and repair, general response to oxidative stress and pH survival in the phagosome (DnaN, Rv0002; RecF, Rv0003; DinF, Rv2836c; Rv3242c, Rv1264) were upregulated (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Among the downregulated genes in Mtb in Plin2-/- macrophages, FurA (Rv1909c), a KatG repressor was the most significant.
source: Among the downregulated genes in Mtb in Plin2-/- macrophages, FurA (Rv1909c), a KatG repressor was the most significant (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: FurA downregulation derepresses the catalase peroxidase, KatG, which promotes Mtb survival in oxidative stress conditions.
source: FurA downregulation derepresses the catalase peroxidase, KatG, which promotes Mtb survival in oxidative stress conditions (Zahrt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zahrt et al., 2001.

claim: The majority of the DE genes in Mtb from Cpt2-/- macrophages (8 out of 10) were also DE in Plin2-/- macrophages.
source: Cpt2-/- macrophages elicited a modest shift in transcriptional response from Mtb, and the majority of the DE genes (8 out of 10) were also DE in Plin2-/- macrophages (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Upregulated genes in Mtb isolated from Cpt2-/- macrophages included those involved in response to oxidative stress (DinF, Rv2836c).
source: In common with the Mtb transcriptome response in Plin2-/- macrophages, upregulated genes in Mtb isolated from Cpt2-/- macrophages included those involved in response to oxidative stress (DinF, Rv2836c) (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: In both infected and uninfected conditions, all three mutants displayed significantly elevated total cellular ROS compared to scramble controls.
source: In both infected and uninfected conditions, all the three mutants displayed significantly elevated total cellular ROS compared to scramble controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy analysis of CellROX-stained cells shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: None of the three lipid metabolism inhibitors had a measurable effect on Mtb growth in liquid culture media compared to DMSO controls.
source: None of the three lipid metabolism inhibitors had a measurable effect on Mtb growth in liquid culture media compared to DMSO controls (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bacterial growth curve data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Treatment with rifampicin completely blocked bacterial growth under the same conditions.
source: Treatment with rifampicin completely blocked bacterial growth under the same conditions (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bacterial growth curve data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: TMZ and metformin significantly reduced bacterial loads in macrophages compared to DMSO controls.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Chandra et al., 2020; Singhal et al., 2014), TMZ and metformin significantly reduced bacterial loads in macrophages compared to DMSO controls (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 8B and is consistent with previous observations cited from Chandra et al., 2020 and Singhal et al., 2014.

claim: FATP1 In impacted the intracellular growth of Mtb.
source: Similarly, FATP1 In also impacted the intracellular growth of Mtb (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A deficiency of CD36 enhances macrophage control of Mtb, albeit to a modest degree.
source: Earlier studies reported that a deficiency of CD36 enhances macrophage control of Mtb, albeit to a modest degree (Hawkes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hawkes et al., 2010.

claim: The antimicrobial effectors in CD36-deficient macrophages were not due to bacterial uptake deficiencies, differences in the rate of Mtb-induced host cell death, and production of ROS or pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Work from Hawkes et al., 2010 indicated that the antimicrobial effectors in CD36-deficient macrophages were not due to bacterial uptake deficiencies, differences in the rate of Mtb-induced host cell death, and production of ROS or pro-inflammatory cytokines (Hawkes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hawkes et al., 2010.

claim: SLC27A1 knockout resulted in the upregulation of other lipid import transporters (MSR1, ABCC1).
source: Indeed, we found out that SLC27A1 knockout resulted in the upregulation of other lipid import transporters (MSR1, ABCC1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Chemical, genetic, or miR33-mediated blockade of fatty acid β-oxidation in macrophages induces lipid droplet formation.
source: It has also been previously reported that chemical, genetic, or miR33-mediated blockade of fatty acid β-oxidation in macrophages induces lipid droplet formation (Chandra et al., 2020; Ouimet et al., 2016) but that this enhanced lipid droplet formation does not correlate with improved intracellular Mtb growth (Chandra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chandra et al., 2020 and Ouimet et al., 2016.

claim: Enhanced lipid droplet formation from blockade of fatty acid β-oxidation does not correlate with improved intracellular Mtb growth.
source: It has also been previously reported that chemical, genetic, or miR33-mediated blockade of fatty acid β-oxidation in macrophages induces lipid droplet formation (Chandra et al., 2020; Ouimet et al., 2016) but that this enhanced lipid droplet formation does not correlate with improved intracellular Mtb growth (Chandra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chandra et al., 2020.

claim: Metformin is a widely used antidiabetic drug that activates AMPK, inhibits fatty acid synthesis, and promotes β-oxidation of fatty acids.
source: Such compounds include metformin, a widely used antidiabetic drug that activates AMPK, inhibits fatty acid synthesis, and promotes β-oxidation of fatty acids (Fullerton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fullerton et al., 2013 and Singhal et al., 2014.
